And every year during this important time, This American Life brings you yet another program about poultry. That's right-- stories about turkeys, chickens, ducks, fowl of all kind, and their mysterious hold over us.

segments.text: It's not unusual for older siblings to dominate younger ones. And as children, Danielle dominated Ashley. Ashley looked up to Danielle, fought to get her attention and her approval, and Danielle always, always got her way. Except when Duki was around.

segments.text: Basically, Ashley would channel-- I mean, the word's kind of an anachronism in this context-- but she would channel Duki. She would become Duki's voice. She would speak as Duki. segments.text: So I hope it's becoming clear why, if you eat dinner in the home of Danielle's family, if they're serving some kind of poultry-- you know, chicken or turkey-- if you were to ask anybody in the family, "what's for dinner," they'll tell you--

segments.text: But of course, this is a city person's perspective, and that means it is completely wrong-headed from the point of view of anybody who actually raises birds. Standing in the cold feed room, I had a long, long talk with George about this. George is 80 years old. He's been raising birds since the-- I guess the Calvin Coolidge administration. And he says the whole fun of raising birds is raising them to the standard.

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: Well, like, for instance, if your birds lack bone, OK, you go out and buy a bird as near to like them as you can with better bone. But when you mate them together, you might get long-legged birds, or too short. I mean, you don't get what you want just by mating. It takes four or five years to gradually get it out, and by that time, they're inbred and you need new ones.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: George tells me that when he's breeding a new batch of birds, he'll hatch 65 of them, and only one or two will be anywhere near the Standard of Perfection. That's how hard it is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you get frustrated with the Standard Of Protection sometimes?

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: No, we get frustrated with the judges. Because every judge has his own idea of what the standard should be.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I thought that's the whole point of a standard, is that--

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: That is. But one judge will want it this way, and another another. Today, if you bred your birds to the standard of perfection-- weight and everything-- and took them to the show, you probably wouldn't get anywhere. You've got to breed to the fads.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's right. The fads. Like Cornishes these days are supposed to have shorter legs than the real Standard of Perfection. Vertical tail feathers are out in all sorts of breeds that really should have them. In the country, among the chicken breeders, they think about a lot of things you never get to in the city.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when you're raising these birds, with any of these birds, do you have a close relationship with a bird the way some do [UNINTELLIGIBLE] with a pet?

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: I don't have time. Yeah, I got too many things to do. See, a few years ago, I almost died of cancer, and the Good Lord told me how to cure myself. And so I've been working with that a lot the last three years. I've been helping people, and put in papers. Now it's getting all over the United States.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What did you do? What do you do?

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: It's you use the root of a dandelion. Simple as can be. But there's something in that that builds up your blood and your immune system.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait a second. You're saying that you were diagnosed with cancer, and this is the only treatment you've had, and it cured you?

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: Yeah. And I've given it to other people when the medical world has told them that there's nothing more they can do, and they've gotten well, too. But not all of them. If they're too far gone, it won't help them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And you make it into tea or something like that?

segments.speaker: George Cairns
segments.text: We just put it in a little water, a little milk, Kool-Aide. You can put it on a sandwich. Anything that isn't hot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: George gives me a pamphlet that he's written up. No doctor has actually checked him out to prove the cancer is gone from his body. He's actually got no hard scientific proof that this really works, but he says God told him that this is the way he should be spending his time. And it has cut into his bird breeding a bit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: George leaves, off on other business. Tamara is finished hanging and lighting the next backdrop. And the rest of us begin with the second bird, a bird called a Brahma, with elaborately patterned brown and white feathers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [BIRD CLUCKING]

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: Got her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She is big. This is a chicken like the size of a dog.

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: Not that big.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A small dog.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our second bird demonstrates the great distance between bird, instinct, and intelligence. And the demands of modern fashion photography, which is to say, of civilization. Called upon to do human tasks, even rather passive ones, a bird remains a bird.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Paul carries the huge hen onto the fragile little set Tamara has built.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: He's a beauty. What ya eating there, buddy?

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: [BIRD SQUAKING]

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Whew, it slapped me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: "I'm scared of this one," she says, quietly, as she adjusts her camera. The chicken is so big-- nine pounds, the size of a small consumer turkey-- that she has to pull the camera back. the Davidsons are looking at her skeptically. Paul asked pointedly if she's ever shot a bird this big.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: We've got to figure out where the--

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: [BIRD SQUACKING]

segments.speaker: Dick Davidson
segments.text: Whoa.

segments.speaker: Dick Davidson
segments.text: [BIRD CLUCKING]

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Hello, bird. Are you going to slap me in the face again? I hope not.

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: [UNINTELLIGIBLE] jump right in your face.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: You know why you're here? Let's talk. We need you to be beautiful. Here's your moment. OK? There are more where you came from, buddy. You better act up here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This combination of coddling and threats might motivate an aspiring supermodel, or an eager puppy. But this, after all, is a chicken. Laura tries to lure it up with a handful of corn.

segments.speaker: Laura Davidson
segments.text: She standing--

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: She can get corn, or she's trying to get it, but she has to stand up high for it.

segments.speaker: Laura Davidson
segments.text: Is that where you want her to stand?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Someone during this ordeal, a funny thing happens. All the Davidsons, who all started off skeptical, they are completely engaged. Dick suggests a pose that is pure art concept, a pose that could not be further from Standard of Perfection. Laura lures the bird with corn, Paul smooths feathers, and when the bird quivers or moves a wing, three people jump in to fix it back up.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: There's some feathers on the breast a little bit. A little bit fluffy. You know, it's like she's not real cleaned on there-- OK. She's a little farther. You guys are a great team. I'm going to hire you to come with me.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Oops, I got a hand in there.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Move the hand, move the hand. Move the hand. OK, great.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It wasn't until this point that I realized that I came into this sort of expecting the bird to be more, well, more human. Partly, I think, because I had never really thought about this one way or the other. But partly because Tamara's photos make chicken seem so thoughtful.

segments.speaker: Laura Davidson
segments.text: [UNINTELLIGIBLE].

segments.speaker: Laura Davidson
segments.text: [PEOPLE CLICKING TO GET BIRD'S ATTENTION]

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: Over here. Look at the camera, look at the camera. Right there.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: No, she's completely out of frame.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Those photos are a lie.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [PEOPLE CLICKING TO GET BIRD'S ATTENTION]

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: I think you're going to have a one shot opportunity here. It's going to be when I let go.

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: [CHICKEN CLUCKING]

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: [WINGS FLUTTERING]

segments.speaker: Paul Davidson
segments.text: Whoa. Geez, I didn't even let go. I just started to let up and he yanked it right out of my hand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Fact is, you can try to give chickens respect. You can try to treat them dignity, and photograph them the way you'd photograph anything or anyone that's serious, but the chickens will not care. You can make them look dignified, but it is a brainless, bird-like dignity, and it is ephemeral.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you feel like your relationship with chicken has changed because of this?

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: No. Not at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How could that not be so?

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Um, I order the chicken when I'm at the show. I eat it right in front of the chickens.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You eat chicken while you're standing there with a chicken?

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Yes. [LAUGHING] Is it wrong? I don't know. I'm hungry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, no wonder they won't sit still.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Tamara Staples
segments.text: [CHICKING CALLING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We pack up our gear and move the massive wall of hay back into place. As we do this, chickens hop by. Brahmas, Americanas, mixed breeds. They seem utterly uninterested in us. They cluck at each other, there's feed to eat, hay to nestle in-- they have better things to do with their time. And you know, there's nothing that makes you realize just how inhuman chickens are than spending a day trying to make them seem human.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [CHICKEN AND COW SOUNDS]
